Sedimentary rock. Rocks formed from the consolidation and lithification of sediments—fragments of rock and minerals produced by weathering, as well as chemical precipitates and organic material—that accumulate in layers at Earth's surface. Sedimentary rocks are the only rock type that commonly contains fossils, making them invaluable for understanding past life and environments. They cover about seventy-five percent of Earth's land surface despite comprising only five percent of the crust by volume.

Sedimentary rocks form in three stages: weathering, the breaking down of existing rocks; transport, the movement of fragments by water, wind, or ice; and lithification, the compaction and cementation of layers into solid rock. Clastic sedimentary rocks are composed of mineral fragments cemented together, with examples including sandstone, made of sand-sized grains, and shale, made of mud-sized clay. Grain size reflects transport distance and energy of the depositional environment. Chemical sedimentary rocks form when dissolved minerals precipitate out of water. Limestone, composed of calcium carbonate, is the quintessential biochemical sedimentary rock, formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms accumulating on the seafloor.

Fossils are preserved in sedimentary rocks because organisms are buried quickly, before decay or scavenging can destroy them. Fossil layers mark distinct time periods and allow scientists to date rocks and correlate strata across continents. Stratigraphy is the study of rock layers. The principle of superposition states that in undisturbed sequences, older rocks lie beneath younger ones, allowing relative dating of fossils and rocks without radiometric methods.

Sedimentary rocks are economically important. They host most oil and natural gas reserves formed from organic-rich shales and limestone, groundwater aquifers, and valuable minerals like salt and phosphate. Cross-bedding and ripple marks are sedimentary features formed by flowing water or wind. These structures reveal the direction and energy of ancient currents and are used to reconstruct past environments.
